Tempête de neige et mobilité réduite :: Snowstorms and reduced mobility: “The reality is, nobody ever thinks of us!”
Alerte tempête à Montréal ! Pour les per: Storm alert in Montréal! For people with reduced mobility, 75 cm of snow exposed serious inequalities.
Les tempêtes de février ont causé énormé: The February storms caused enormous chaos in Montréal, and the slow snow removal that followed was on everyone’s lips. During my time at École Converse, we were asked to write an article on a subject of our choice. I started out with the idea of writing about the lack of accessibility in Montréal, or about the inequalities in snow removal services that some communities suffer from.
Sur le terrain, une chose revenait souve: Out in the field, one thing kept coming up in conversations: worry for seniors and for people with disabilities or reduced mobility. Hearing those concerns, this issue imposed itself on me.
Un témoignage en particulier m’est resté: One account in particular stayed with me: my mother told me about a family friend who, after the big storms, decided to move into a seniors’ residence. Not just because clearing the snow was too much work, but also because he realized how much he depended on other people and on weather conditions for his basic needs, like getting to the grocery store or the pharmacy.
La Ville de Montréal a promis de doubler: The City of Montréal has promised to double its level of accessibility by 2030, but the February storms and the accounts gathered in the field showed that there is still a long way to go.
<strong>En février dernier, Montréal a c: Last February, Montréal experienced an unprecedented situation. Over three days, the city received nearly 75 cm of snow, an exceptional event not seen since the 1950s, according to Valérie Plante, the mayor of Montréal. This record, the result of a series of heavy storms, brought the city’s streets to a standstill. But the thick blanket of snow also revealed deep inequalities among residents.
<strong>25 février.</strong> Alors que l: February 25. As darkness falls on the streets of Montréal, the sound of snowplows and light rain can be heard. The atmosphere is soothed by the gentle melting of the snow that piled up during the last two icy storms. Paths have been dug through the recently buried streets and sidewalks of Montréal. People cheerfully show their faces again after several days hidden away in the warmth... But for some, the relief is mixed.
Alors que nous parcourons les rues de Mo: As we walk the streets of Montréal to assess the situation, a woman walking with a cane stops us. She asks whether the route we just took is safe. If she falls, she says, she might not get back up. Like her, many Montrealers get around with difficulty.
<strong>Neige après neige, des chez-soi: Snowfall after snowfall, homes that are crumbling
« Ces tempêtes m’ont beaucoup dérangé. M: “These storms disturbed me a lot. My daily routine wasn’t the same anymore. My activities came to a halt,” he says in a calm but upset voice. “I couldn’t leave my house without assistance until the sidewalks had been cleared.”
D’ordinaire, Nemours se rend à l’épiceri: Normally, Nemours walks to the grocery store and the pharmacy. But this time, the snow and ice make going out too risky. He now depends on his fellow parishioners to bring him food and whatever else he needs. So he waits, isolated at home, for the city to regain some semblance of accessibility.
Nemours a tenté de déneiger lui-même son: Nemours tried to clear the snow from his balcony and his parking spot himself. After the first storm, he looked for help, but in vain. So he did the snow removal himself, at the risk of getting hurt, which is what ended up happening, he tells us. While trying to lift the snow, he hurt his back. It was only after the second storm that he finally received help from his children.
Ces malheureux épisodes lui rappellent q: These unfortunate episodes remind him that maintaining his home, his refuge since he arrived in Canada in 1974, is becoming a daily struggle. Each storm pushes him further toward an idea he has avoided for years: leaving his home for a seniors’ residence.
‍<strong>Coincés par la neige, privés de: ‍Trapped by the snow, cut off from essential resources
‍<strong>3 mars.</strong> De l’autre côt: ‍March 3. On the other side of the city, people with reduced mobility face the same accessibility problems, like Avi Karp, who lives in L’Île-Bizard. A representative of the New Democratic Party (NDP) for people with disabilities, he advocates for a more inclusive society.
La voix gaie et le rire facile, il recon: With a cheerful voice and an easy laugh, he readily acknowledges that the latest storms were completely unprecedented. A mess like no other and something never seen before, in his own words. For lack of options, enough workers and adequate planning, streets and sidewalks are being used improperly, which puts everyone at risk.
« Je suis correct pour marcher jusqu’à l: “I’m fine to walk to the grocery store if I really need to. But what about the people who can’t? Those who are in wheelchairs and stuck in their apartments, those who are retired and don’t have much money, or any at all, to spend on their basic needs… Especially with the cost of living being so high. I think about those people.”
Avi dépend des banques alimentaires. Tou: Avi depends on food banks. However, with the amount of snow that fell, no food deliveries had taken place for days. For those who, like him, depend on these services and live with a disability, this can be very problematic, especially if they live alone or have no support.
<strong>3 mars.</strong> Sur le Plateau,: March 3. On the Plateau, where you might think the situation is better, the reality is no rosier. Parking spots for people with reduced mobility are turned into snow dumps to free up parking lots, and accessibility ramps are buried and forgotten under the snow. Many Montrealers are therefore forced to stay home, hoping they have enough resources to meet their needs.
C’est ce dont parle Allie Pauld, créatri: That is what Allie Pauld, a content creator and disability activist, talks about in one of her recent educational videos posted on Instagram: “Many disabled people risk being confined to their homes for weeks, which means having to ration their food and pay exorbitant prices for essential deliveries.”
Pour ce qui est d’Allie, son père la pré: As for Allie, her father warns her every time an episode of extreme weather is about to hit, which lets her prepare and stock up in her apartment: food, hygiene products and everything she needs to hold out. That way, she stayed holed up at home from mid-February until the end of the month, waiting for the storms to pass and for the city to finally become accessible again.
Mais qu’en est-il des personnes qui n’on: But what about people who have neither support nor loved ones to warn them and help them prepare for these extreme conditions?
Avi reconnaît qu’il est privilégié. Lors: Avi acknowledges that he is privileged. When people with reduced mobility are stuck at home, they are cut off from their loved ones, friends, families, partners and even the organizations they depend on, he points out. “Me, I have support systems in person, by phone, online... Things like that. But again, if you’re retired or you have a disability, if you have a modest income, those resources are sometimes simply out of reach.”
<strong>Neige, obstacles et indifférence: Snow, obstacles and indifference: who is responsible?
Allie souhaiterait quant à elle que les: Allie, for her part, would like Montréal residents to understand how crucial the issue of accessibility is.
C’est le troisième hiver qu’elle passe d: This is her third winter in the city, and like every year, it’s a fight. The maintenance worker at her building takes care of clearing the stairs and opening a path to the sidewalk. The City takes care of clearing the sidewalk. But in between, no one clears the space between the access ramp and the curb. The maintenance worker believes it is the City’s responsibility, while the City thinks it is up to the maintenance worker. Allie is left with an inaccessible ramp and a wheelchair stuck in the snow.
« Beaucoup considèrent ces aménagements: “Many people see these accommodations as extra spaces they can use whenever they feel like it, for fun. In reality, they meet essential needs and were won through the relentless efforts of those who absolutely need them,” adds Allie, visibly upset.
D’autres infrastructures importantes, co: Other important infrastructure, like the access ramps on buses, can only be used if the space is cleared. Too often, the authorities don’t bother to clear the snow at these stops, making them unusable for people who use a wheelchair, like Allie.
Ayant un accès limité, voire impossible,: With limited or even no access to public transit during the winter, she nevertheless pays full fare for her OPUS card, like everyone else. The services are not adapted to her needs, and no one seems to take responsibility for this lack of inclusivity.
« Les gens pensent que, parce que nous s: “People think that because we have reduced mobility, we never go out in bad weather. But we still have to go grocery shopping, buy shampoo, go to work, pick up our kids from school… We have the same needs and the same responsibilities as everyone else, except our needs aren’t taken into account. In the end, we fall through the cracks of the system, where no one takes responsibility for supporting us.”
<strong>Le déneigement à Montréal : un s: Snow removal in Montréal: a service that is “extremely important for human rights”
Selon Craig Sauvé, conseiller municipal: According to Craig Sauvé, a city councillor in the Sud-Ouest borough for more than 10 years, the city of Montréal came very close to a state of natural disaster during the latest storms, and people need to take that into account.
Il reconnaît les défis que pose le dénei: He acknowledges the challenges of snow removal, but points out that financial and logistical constraints limit the City’s ability to act.
« Lorsque nous effectuons des opérations: “When we carry out regular snow removal operations for accumulations of 15 cm, it costs the City of Montréal about $25 million. It mobilizes around 3,000 employees, sometimes even 3,500. There are about 400 tow trucks moving cars to clear the lanes. So it’s a very big operation. And the storm we just had was huge,” he says.
À la question de savoir si la Ville a re: Asked whether the City has received complaints about winter accessibility, he answers frankly and without hesitation that it has.
Des groupes comme Ex aequo et le Regroup: Groups like Ex aequo and the Regroupement des activistes pour l’inclusion au Québec (RAPLIQ) are indeed very concerned about the issue. The City has received complaints and letters from advocacy groups about seasonal and general accessibility, which Sauvé calls healthy and useful pressure. “It pushes public works officials to stay vigilant and to improve their services.”
Les échanges de Craig Sauvé avec des aîn: Craig Sauvé’s conversations with seniors and with people who have reduced mobility or low vision have shown him how much the harshness of the climate can significantly affect their lives in a very short time.
« Il y a de la place pour beaucoup d’amé: “There is room for a lot of improvement,” he concedes. “Snow removal is a basic service that is extremely important for human rights in Montréal.”
Des zones prioritaires ont désormais été: Priority zones have now been added for snow removal, including in front of seniors’ residences, hospitals, clinics, public spaces, daycares, schools, school zones, bus stops and main arteries. These priorities are being put in place and are improving, he says.
Avec les événements du début de l’hiver,: With the events of early winter, Allie hopes the past few weeks will act as a wake-up call. “The reality is, nobody ever thinks of us!” she exclaims. “No one takes charge of accessibility, because everyone thinks it’s someone else’s job.”
L’accessibilité ne se limite pas aux dép: Accessibility isn’t limited to getting around or public transit; it is tied to every aspect of daily life. “When people with reduced mobility explain that they can’t go into most cafés, live in most apartments or buy a house because of the lack of accessibility, we’re told it’s our bodies that aren’t working the way they should, that it’s a personal problem. But in reality, it’s a real concern that should be taken seriously and fixed.”
L’accessibilité ne devrait pas être un l: Accessibility should not be a luxury but a fundamental right, and Allie, Avi and Nemours insist on this point throughout our conversations. For these three citizens, it is inconceivable to view as a favour or an exception what should be the norm. It is not a matter of comfort or convenience, but a matter of dignity, autonomy and freedom.
